cues.text: A Scholar Formed by Rome and the Desert
Born around 347 at Stridon, on the border between Dalmatia and Pannonia, Jerome received the finest classical education Rome could offer.
Mastering Latin rhetoric and literature, he developed a passion that would remain with him, for better and for worse, his whole life.
Baptized in Rome as a young man, he traveled restlessly through Gaul and the East.
In his early thirties, he withdrew into the harsh Syrian desert, where he lived for several years as a hermit.
Determined to master the discipline of asceticism, he pursued it as thoroughly as he had already mastered classical letters.
It was in this same desert period that Jerome experienced the dream he would later describe with unforgettable vividness.

He stood before Christ’s judgment seat, accused of loving pagan literature more than sacred Scripture and scourged for this fault—a vision so searing that he vowed from that day never again to read the classical authors he had loved.
By his own admission, he would keep that vow only imperfectly, but it permanently reoriented the whole direction of his scholarship.
Secretary to a Pope
Returning to Rome in 382, Jerome became secretary and close theological advisor to Pope Damasus I .
Damasus set him the task that would occupy much of the rest of his life.
It was to produce a reliable, unified Latin translation of the Scriptures to replace the confusing, inconsistent array of Old Latin versions then in circulation.
Jerome's years in Rome also brought him into close spiritual friendship with a circle of aristocratic Roman women.
These women were drawn to serious study of Scripture and to ascetic life, and their patronage and companionship would sustain his scholarly work for decades.
However, his blunt criticism of the moral laxity he saw among some of the Roman clergy also earned him powerful enemies, and when Damasus died in 384, Jerome found Rome no longer hospitable to him.
Thirty-Four Years in a Cave
In 386, Jerome withdrew permanently to Bethlehem , settling into a cave beneath the very grotto traditionally venerated as the site of Christ's birth.
There, he founded a monastery and, alongside it, a community of nuns under the direction of his friend and patroness Paula.
There, for the next thirty-four years, he pursued the great labor of his life: a fresh Latin translation of the entire Old Testament directly from the original Hebrew .
This was a startling and, to many contemporaries, controversial departure from the established practice of translating only from the Greek Septuagint.
Jerome was convinced that the truest meaning of Scripture could only be reached by returning, wherever possible, to its very first written form.
The resulting translation, together with his earlier revision of the Gospels, became known over the following centuries as the Vulgate .
It was so named because it rendered Scripture into the vulgar, that is, the common everyday Latin every literate person of the age could read.
The Vulgate would remain the Church's standard biblical text for well over a thousand years.
A Temper as Sharp as His Scholarship

Jerome's genuine holiness never fully smoothed over a naturally combative temperament, and his surviving letters show a man capable of ferocious, sometimes uncharitable polemic against those he judged theologically or morally wanting.
A public and painful controversy with his former friend Rufinus, and sharp exchanges even with the great Augustine of Hippo, strained Jerome’s later years.
Augustine sought through his letters—though not always successfully—to resolve the misunderstandings between two of the Latin Church’s greatest minds.
We do well not to pretend this side of Jerome away; rather, we should see in it a reminder.
Even the saints remain, to the end, imperfect vessels wrestling with their own temperament.
God can use, and even sanctify, gifts and flaws together, so long as the heart beneath them remains truly given to him.
Compassion in a Collapsing World
When Rome itself fell to the Visigoths in 410, shockwaves of grief and confusion swept through the whole Christian world.
Jerome, now an old man in distant Bethlehem, set aside his beloved scholarly labors to help receive and care for refugees fleeing the disaster.
He wrote that he had put aside all his study because now was a time for weeping, not for words.
It was proof that even the most single-minded scholar of his generation understood that love of neighbor could, when the moment demanded it, take precedence even over love of the sacred text.
Legacy
Jerome died in Bethlehem on 30 September 420, having given the Latin-speaking Church, in a single lifetime's labor, the Bible it would read, pray, and study for the next millennium and a half.
Counted among the four great Doctors of the Latin Church alongside Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory the Great, Jerome is honored as the patron of translators, librarians, and biblical scholars.
His life stands as an enduring testament to a truth he himself once put more sharply than perhaps any other Christian writer: ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ .
And no labor, however difficult or however long, is too great a price to pay for placing God's own word directly into the hands of his people.
